clue.text: Smooth wrapping paper, easily damaged?

indicators.note: the smoothing word wraps around the paper word, holding it in its middle

parts.note: to file something is to smooth it with a rasp
a rag is slang for a newspaper

explanation.surface: A parcel in smooth wrapping paper, with a guess that it might be easily damaged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fragile breaks easily, so is easily damaged; the question mark nods to parcels labelled that way.

clue.text: Those in the red hats initially stuffing turkey in retail establishment

indicators.note: stuffing puts the debtors and the letter inside the failure word

parts.note: a turkey is a failure, a flop
people in the red owe money, so are owers

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of hats

explanation.surface: A Christmas scene: shoppers in red hats stuffing a turkey in a store.
explanation.definitionFit: A florist's is a retail establishment, a store selling blooms.

clue.text: A Norway spruce in part of Northern Ireland

parts.note: N is the international vehicle code for Norway
spruce and trim both mean neat

explanation.surface: A Norway spruce tree growing somewhere in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Norway spruce' looks like the tree; it splits into a country code and an adjective meaning neat.
explanation.definitionFit: Antrim is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, on its north-east coast.

clue.text: Man in life, flawed genius primarily, as writer

indicators.note: flawed suggests something damaged out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
primarily takes the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A man whose life showed flawed genius, above all as an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flawed' rearranges MANINLIFE into IANFLEMIN; 'primarily' adds G.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Fleming was the British novelist who created James Bond.

clue.text: Cardinal virtue finally turning up, little time to live

indicators.note: turning up in a down entry means the pieces read from bottom to top

parts.note: six is a cardinal number

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of virtue

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A cardinal's virtue finally comes to light, with little time left to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal virtue' looks like prudence or justice; 'turning up' reverses SIXE to EXIS.
explanation.definitionFit: To exist is to be alive, to have being.

clue.text: Sprout inspiring celebrated bird

indicators.note: inspiring means breathing in, so the sprout word takes the other inside it

parts.note: a bud is a sprouting shoot
a star is a celebrated person

explanation.surface: A sprouting plant gives life to a famous bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The bustard is a large ground-dwelling game bird of open plains.

clue.text: Game all I cooked in partridges etc

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters within the other word

parts.note: partridges are one example of birds

indicators.note: cooked means falsified or messed about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Game birds: everything I cooked went into the partridges and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like the shot birds, but it is the definition; 'cooked' makes LLIA from the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Billiards is a cue game played on a cloth-covered table.

clue.text: See 1
Advise against a plate of food Boxing Day

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing, so the dish wraps round the day

parts.note: a dish is a plate of food
Mon is short for Monday, a day

explanation.surface: A warning against a plate of food on Boxing Day.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing Day is the British holiday on 26 December; here 'Boxing' tells A DISH to box MON.
explanation.definitionFit: To admonish is to warn or caution someone against doing something.

clue.text: Foppish behaviour in mind say, dude's first to gyrate

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the dude word
to gyrate is to spin round, so the letters are whirled into a new order

explanation.surface: A dandy dude is first to spin round in a show of foppishness.
explanation.walkthrough: MINDSAY plus D are rearranged by 'to gyrate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dandyism is the dress and manner of a dandy, a man obsessed with elegant clothes.

clue.text: Oliver Twist, perhaps, in the Queen's Speech on a regular basis

indicators.note: the royal, very clipped accent is said to make the orphan word come out with a different sound

parts.note: Dickens's Oliver Twist is the classic orphan

explanation.surface: Dickens's boy hero is mentioned regularly in the monarch's Christmas broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen's Speech is the monarch's Christmas Day broadcast in Britain; the joke is that a very posh accent says 'orphan' as 'orfen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means frequently, happening on a regular basis.

clue.text: British dependency no good for flamingoes in a storm

indicators.note: a storm throws the remaining letters into a wild new order
no good says the good letter is to be taken away from the birds

explanation.surface: A British territory is no good for flamingoes when the weather turns stormy.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing G from FLAMINGOES leaves FLAMINOES, which 'in a storm' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is a Crown dependency, self-governing but under the British Crown.

clue.text: Spot recalled into which hefty eater takes a great deal — that's behind the tongue

indicators.note: into which says the following pieces go inside the turned spot word
recalled is read as called back, so the spot word runs backwards

parts.note: a site is a spot or location
a pig is a greedy, hefty eater
a lot is a great deal, which the eater takes as its helping

explanation.surface: A spot is remembered where a glutton grabs plenty, apparently at the back of the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns the spot word around to ETIS, which then splits open to hold the eater and the great deal.
explanation.definitionFit: The epiglottis is the flap at the root of the tongue that covers the windpipe when swallowing.

clue.text: Popular daily, vacuous newspaper in short?

parts.note: in means popular or fashionable

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its middle and only its ends stay

explanation.surface: A popular daily paper dismissed as vacuous and briefly named.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indy is the familiar short name for The Independent, a British national paper.

clue.text: Box clever in the end, entering school as writer

parts.note: a chest is a box

indicators.note: entering says the letter goes inside the school name

parts.note: Eton is the famous English public school

indicators.note: in the end takes the final letter of clever

explanation.surface: A box, cleverly sent to school, becomes an author.
explanation.definitionFit: G K Chesterton was the English author of the Father Brown stories.

clue.text: Christmas crackers to grip on, those for Elizabeth?

indicators.note: to grip says the jumbled letters hold the next word inside them
crackers means crazy, so the festive word is jumbled

explanation.surface: Festive crackers to pull and keep a grip on, perhaps the sort that are pro-Elizabeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crackers' scrambles the festive word into MARCHISTS, whose M is then split by the gripped word.
explanation.definitionFit: Monarchists support the monarchy, so they are in favour of a queen such as Elizabeth II.

clue.text: Make dull creations lively

indicators.note: lively suggests jumping about, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Turning lively creations into dull ones.
explanation.definitionFit: To narcotise is to drug, numbing the senses into dullness.

clue.text: A newspaper I love in outskirts of Chilean capital

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

indicators.note: in puts the self and the zero inside the picked letters
outskirts means the outermost letters of the word

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A newspaper declares its love for the outskirts of the Chilean capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chilean capital' suggests Santiago, but the answer is Paraguay's capital; Chilean only gives C and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Asuncion is the capital city of Paraguay.

clue.text: What's up high, punched by old boxer?

indicators.note: punched by says the old letter is driven into the jumbled letters
high means intoxicated, so the letters are wildly rearranged

explanation.surface: A greeting to someone high up, before an old boxer punches them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxer' looks like a dog; 'high' turns WHATSUP into SUTHPAW, which O enters after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A southpaw is a left-handed boxer, leading with the right.

clue.text: Those making rowdy brawls from fairy lights, perhaps?

definitions.text: Those making rowdy brawls from fairy lights, perhaps?

parts.words: Those making rowdy brawls from fairy lights, perhaps?
parts.note: swap the opening sounds of fairy lights and you get lairy fights, which are rowdy brawls

explanation.surface: Christmas decorations seem to start drunken punch-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: Lairy is British slang for loud and aggressive, so lairy fights are rowdy brawls; fairy lights are Christmas string lights.
explanation.definitionFit: Swapping initial sounds of two words is the slip named after Reverend William Spooner of Oxford.

clue.text: Scrooge investing capital in theory — that's how he's known

indicators.note: investing means clothing or surrounding, so the miser word wraps round the letter

parts.note: Dickens's Scrooge is the archetypal miser

indicators.note: capital in means the first, capital letter of theory

explanation.surface: Scrooge investing his money, in theory; that is his title.
explanation.definitionFit: Mister is the title by which a man is addressed, as in Mr Scrooge.

clue.text: Wilder verbal attack starts in European city

parts.note: Gene Wilder was the American comic actor

indicators.note: starts takes the opening letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: A wilder verbal attack begins in a European city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilder' looks like a comparative adjective; it is the actor Gene Wilder.
explanation.definitionFit: Geneva is the Swiss city on Lake Geneva.

clue.text: Crackers — what are they for?

definitions.meaning: asks what nutcrackers are meant to crack open

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about the purpose of Christmas crackers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts is slang for mad, and nutcrackers exist to open the shelled kernels.

clue.text: Censor wicked and loathsome extremists heading for Richmond in US state capital

indicators.note: in puts the picked letters inside the city name

parts.note: Boise is the capital of Idaho

indicators.note: extremists here means the outer letters of each of the two words
heading for takes just the opening letter of the place name

explanation.surface: A censor condemns wicked, loathsome extremists bound for Richmond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremists' looks like people; it means the end letters of the two words before it. Boise is the capital of Idaho.
explanation.definitionFit: To bowdlerise is to censor a text by cutting supposedly offensive parts, after Thomas Bowdler's expurgated Shakespeare.

clue.text: Ultimately, reverie in short?

indicators.note: in puts the picked letter inside the drink word

parts.note: a short is a small measure of spirits, a dram

indicators.note: ultimately takes the closing letter of the musing word

explanation.surface: A daydream of, in the end, a nip of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' is British pub talk for a measure of spirits; the whole clue doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a fanciful musing, the waking vision of the mind.

clue.text: Down which Father Christmas sped, did you say?

indicators.note: did you say marks the word as heard rather than seen

parts.note: sped means went fast, flew

explanation.surface: Asking whether Santa raced down something.
explanation.definitionFit: A flue is a chimney duct, the route Santa traditionally takes into the house.

clue.text: Hasty devil, posh as it happens, scoffing last of vol-au-vents

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
U is the old label for upper-class, posh usage

indicators.note: scoffing means gobbling up, so the broadcast word swallows the final letter

parts.note: live describes something broadcast as it happens

indicators.note: last of takes the closing letter of the pastries

explanation.surface: A posh little devil hastily wolfs party pastries in real time.
explanation.definitionFit: Impulsive means acting on a sudden urge without thought, so hasty.

clue.text: Tax contributing to development, it helps

indicators.note: contributing to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A levy that funds development, it is said, helps things along.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a tenth of produce or income paid as a church levy.

clue.text: Christmas present in obscurity

parts.note: on the day itself Christmas is the present moment, now
present means in this place, here

explanation.surface: A Christmas gift lies hidden away somewhere unseen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christmas present' reads as a gift, but splits into two words: the time it is, and being in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is unknown or overlooked is said to be in no place at all, as in came from obscurity.

clue.text: Little time on Whale Island

parts.note: min is short for minute, a little time
the orca is the killer whale

explanation.surface: A short stay on Whale Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Minorca, or Menorca, is one of Spain's Balearic Islands.
